note: Purposive "might gradually acquire" was turned into a flat past-tense assertion.
replacement: I should not have chosen to live in a republic of recent founding, however excellent its laws. I should have feared that the government, perhaps framed differently from what the circumstances of the moment required, might not suit the new citizens, or they might not suit it, and that the State would risk overthrow and destruction almost as soon as it came into being. For liberty is like those solid and succulent foods, or those generous wines, that nourish and strengthen robust constitutions used to them, but ruin and intoxicate weak and delicate constitutions not suited to them. Peoples once accustomed to masters are unable to do without them. If they try to shake off the yoke, they only estrange themselves further from freedom. They mistake for freedom an unbridled license that is its exact opposite, and almost always, through their revolutions, they deliver themselves to seducers who make their chains heavier than before. The Roman people itself, a model for all free peoples, was wholly incapable of governing itself when it escaped the oppression of the Tarquins. It had been debased by slavery and by the ignominious tasks imposed on it, and at first it was no better than a stupid mob, which had to be controlled and governed with the greatest wisdom. Only so could it grow accustomed, by degrees, to breathe the health-giving air of liberty, and its minds, enervated or rather brutalized under tyranny, might gradually acquire that severity of morals and spirit of fortitude which would finally make it the most respectable of all peoples. I should, then, have looked for a peaceful and happy Republic as my country, one of such antiquity that it was lost, as it were, in the night of time. It would have suffered only such shocks as served to show and strengthen the courage and patriotism of its subjects. Its citizens, long accustomed to a wise independence, would have been not only free but worthy to be so.

note: The source parenthetical, which the style note says to keep, was dissolved into separate sentences.
replacement: May a Republic so wisely and happily constituted last for ever, as an example to other nations and for the felicity of its own citizens! This is the only prayer you have left to make, the only precaution that remains to be taken. For the future it depends on yourselves alone (not to make you happy, for your ancestors have saved you that trouble), but to make that happiness lasting, by your wisdom in enjoying it. Your preservation depends on your constant union, your obedience to the laws and your respect for their ministers. If the smallest trace of bitterness or distrust remains among you, hasten to destroy it, as an accursed leaven that sooner or later must bring misfortune and ruin on the State. I conjure you all to look into your hearts and to hearken to the secret voice of conscience. Can any of you find, throughout the universe, a more upright, more enlightened and more honorable body than your magistracy? Do not all its members set you an example of moderation, of simplicity of manners, of respect for the laws and of the most sincere harmony? Place, therefore, without reserve, that salutary confidence in such wise superiors which reason ever owes to virtue. Consider that they are your own choice, that they justify that choice, and that the honors due to those you have dignified are necessarily yours by reflection. Not one of you is so ignorant as not to know that when the laws lose their force, and those who defend them lose their authority, security and liberty are universally impossible. Why, then, should you hesitate to do cheerfully and with just confidence what your true interest, your duty and reason itself would have bound you to do all along?

note: "They have chosen you, men capable of governing others" makes the magistrates the capable men; in the source the electors are.
replacement: And you, most honorable and magnificent lords, the worthy and revered magistrates of a free people, permit me to offer you in particular my duty and homage. If there is a station in the world that can confer honor on those who fill it, it is undoubtedly the one that virtue and talents combine to bestow, the one you have made yourselves worthy of and to which your fellow-citizens have raised you. Their worth adds a new luster to your own. You have been chosen, by men capable of governing others, to govern themselves, and so I cannot but hold you as much superior to all other magistrates as a free people, and particularly the one over which you have the honor to preside, is superior by its wisdom and its reason to the populace of other States.
